name: Raul Alfonso Guerrero
location: Born in Cartagena, Colombia — now in Canada
radio: 500+ radios over a lifetime — nearly 100 still in active collection, all working and looking like new
antenna: Indoor and outdoor configurations — reviews and tests both
favorite_freq: Voice of Free China (Radio Taiwan International) — where the true passion began
why: At age four I picked up my father's transistor radio and accidentally switched it to SW. Turning the dial, I heard voices in completely unfamiliar languages and grasped that the signal was coming from far away. My brother and I each received a radio the following Christmas — single band MW models made in Hong Kong. It was exciting to pick up stations from the Caribbean islands and Florida at night. The true passion began one night while using a four-band radio cassette player — I heard a female voice, Maria Francisca, broadcasting for The Voice of Free China, known today as Radio Taiwan International. During the program they read the mailing address on air. The next day I sent a letter. Two months later I received a large envelope filled with magazines, stickers, pennants, and my first QSL card. I had no idea stations replied to mail. It was a wonderful surprise. Using some savings I bought my first dedicated shortwave radio — a National RF-9L, the smallest on the market at the time. It was the Cold War era, the golden age of shortwave, when the conflict was fought not with bombs but with the ideological propaganda of each side. I wrote to every station I could pick up and happily they all replied with QSL cards and souvenirs. There were also contests with fabulous prizes — ranging from shortwave radios to trips to the station's home country.
best_catch: More than 500 radios have passed through my hands since that first National RF-9L. I still keep nearly 100 of them — all working and looking like new. Today I share my experience with radio listeners around the world through Facebook groups, WhatsApp groups, and my YouTube channel, where I review new radios, cover innovations, and post real-world reception tests using various radios and antennas. Radio faces threats from new technologies and the cost of keeping stations on the air — but I firmly believe radio is here to stay. It has done so much good for humanity and in my own case has transported me to new cultures, languages, and knowledge. Long live radio!
